records.title: Shared Resource Management
records.description:
PROJECT SUMMARY: Shared Resource Management
Shared resource (SR) management ensures formalized planning, actions, and evaluation for members to receive
state-of-the-art, dependable, cost-effective, high-quality services that enhance scientific productivity and
collaboration. CCIL supports three established SRs, with an additional one planned to comprehensively span its
"discovery-to-use" paradigm. Three established SRs characterize cancer's spatial, molecular, and functional
nature: (1) Tumor Engineering and Phenotyping (TEP), a one-stop shop for centralized, assured biological
materials, protocols, and professional services; (2) Carver Biotechnology Center (CBC), providing
comprehensive bioanalytical capability; and, (3) Multimodal Biomedical Imaging (MBI), enabling extensive
multiscale and multi-capability imaging tools. In addition to physical resources, professional staff assist members
in protocol development, experimental design, statistical analyses, and quality assurance. An Associate Director
(AD-SR) oversees SR management, emphasizing CCIL priorities and members in SR use, reporting, and
planning. Joseph Irudayaraj, a highly productive researcher with prior experience administering shared facilities
at an NCI-designated Basic Cancer Center, serves as the AD-SR. The CCIL Administrative Core Team helps
assess instrumentation, services, and staff expertise. They gather feedback from members at program meetings,
working group events, and annual retreats, as well as use quantitative tools like member surveys, usage by
(peer-reviewed) projects, use in publications, and relevance to collaborative, multi-PI cancer projects. Irudayaraj
actively seeks input and responds to members as well as gathers input from SR advisory committees. He shares
performance evaluations and plans at SR townhalls, annual retreats, and CCIL advisory committee meetings.
He coordinates center-wide deliberations related to SRs in monthly meetings of the CCIL Steering Committee
and finalizes actions with the Director. Under Irudayaraj's proactive leadership, SR management has built a new
SR, prioritized acquiring new resources, aided fundraising, and organized instrumentation proposals. These
efforts have been remarkably successful in providing new capabilities and opportunities for members. Since the
last submission, for example, TEP has become fully operational. SR management organized its concept,
developed plans, and submitted a proposal for NIH funding that received a perfect score of 10. Today, the TEP
serves 48% of members; supports T32 training grants, workshops, and summer schools; and has enabled
innovative projects that coalesce CCIL members’ unique capabilities, such as producing tumor organoids using
digital manufacturing concepts. In consultation with the CCIL leadership and program leaders, SR Management
is planning the Prototyping Cancer Innovations (PCI) SR that will assist turning member discoveries into scalable,
testable prototypes of new technologies, molecules with anticancer potential, and advanced software. PCI will
be housed in new CCIL physical space expansion. With a successful track record and plans, SR Management
will continue to provide exceptional support for the growth and increasing impact of CCIL research and education.

records.title: Functional Characterization of the Genetic and Environmental Determinants of Complex Traits
records.description:
Abstract
 Understanding the molecular and organismal function of genetic variants in non-coding regions is crucial to
dissect the genetic and evolutionary basis of variation in complex traits. As we and others have shown, the effect
of a genetic variant on a molecular pathway, and ultimately on the individual's phenotype, may be modulated
by the environmental context (gene-environment interactions, GxE). Most contexts considered to date focus
on aspects of the physical environment that can be reproduced in vitro (e.g., pathogen particles, hormones,
toxicants). We also pioneered the study of GxE with psychosocial experiences (e.g., socio-economic status,
neighborhood stress). Importantly, psychosocial experiences can inﬂuence an individual's ability to respond to
other environmental challenges and these effects can be measured at the cellular level. However the effects
of psychosocial experiences on the transcriptional response to cellular stressors has not been fully evaluated.
The response to environmental challenges is often mediated by changes in transcription factor activity. Single
cell genomics technology has allowed us to discover that gene regulatory changes in response to environmental
perturbations are often heterogeneous both across cell types, and across individual cells within a cell type,
resulting in a dynamic response. This dynamic response can in turn be regulated through GxE, and it's an
important contributor to disease risk. To study the dynamic gene regulatory response to chemical and social
stressors, here we will focus on peripheral blood mononuclear cells from an inner city cohort of middle-aged
adults collected as part of The Heart of Detroit Study (THDS) and consider psychosocial and cellular stressors.
One of the main objectives of this project will be to develop functional genomics, computational, and statistical
approaches to dissect the epigenetic mechanisms underlying the response to in vitro and in vivo stressors, their
interactions with genetic variants, and ultimately their role in complex trait variation. The tools developed in this
project will have broad applicability in the ﬁelds of functional genomics, systems biology, and GxE, ultimately
allowing for a global and integrative analysis of genetic and environmental effects on biological systems.
